interactions.summary: Jiang turns the sewn eyes of the envious into a practical moral psychology: blocked comparison can become either self-work or intensified jealousy depending on whether the soul is purgatorial or hellish.

claims.claim: Jiang accepts that the immediate purpose of shutting the envious person's eyes is to stop obsessive comparison with others.
Jiang ratifies the idea that once comparison is blocked in purgatory, the soul can turn inward and work on itself rather than compete with neighbors.
Hellish envy would invert the same deprivation by making the person continue imagining other people's superiority without any corresponding self-reform.

signature_moments.moment: The class turns envy's cure into a simple formula: stop comparing and work on yourself, but not in order to beat the other guy.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you work on yourself to make yourself better
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It translates Dante's punishment into everyday moral psychology.

signature_moments.moment: Hell is imagined as comparison without reflection, jealousy without transformation.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you still don't look at yourself and try to better yourself
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This sharpens the lecture's recurrent claim that attitude determines whether suffering purifies or corrodes.

chronology_notes.note: Jiang is now explicitly translating the terrace-of-envy imagery into the same punishment/opportunity distinction he used for hell and purgatory more generally.
